The Pragmatic Programmer

David Thomas and Andrew Hunt

The Pragmatic Programmer is a book of practical advice for developers, organized as 53 short, self-contained topics grouped into nine chapters and a postface. Topics cross-reference each other, so the book can be read in any order (Preface to the Second Edition, pp. 17–20). The advice is distilled into 100 numbered tips, set off in boxes in the text. Many topics end with exercises, whose possible answers are in an appendix, and open-ended challenges (p. 20).

The second edition, published twenty years after the first, is a "Ship of Theseus" rewrite: about a third of the topics are new and most of the rest were rewritten (p. 18). The first edition's preface, reprinted from p. 26, sets out the attitude behind the whole book:

  • Tip 1, Care About Your Craft, and Tip 2, Think! About Your Work (p. 30).
  • Continuous small improvement, kaizen (p. 33).

How the book fits together

The chapters move outward from the individual to the project:

  • Chapter 1 sets out the philosophy (responsibility, entropy, good-enough software, learning, communication).
  • Chapter 2 gives the design principles the rest of the book leans on: ETC, DRY, orthogonality, reversibility, tracer bullets and estimating.
  • Chapters 3–6 are the developer's toolkit and defences: tools, paranoia, decoupling and concurrency.
  • Chapter 7 is about the act of coding.
  • Chapters 8–9 cover requirements, agility and teams.
  • The postface turns to ethics.

The arrows are the vault's reading of the cross-references between topics; the chapter order is the book's.

Some threads run through the whole book:

  • Easier to Change (ETC) is the value behind DRY, orthogonality, decoupling, refactoring and agility (2, 5, 7, 8).
  • Feedback loops connect tracer bullets and prototypes, "don't outrun your headlights," testing, requirements and the agile recipe (2, 4, 7, 8).
  • Broken windows and boiled frogs apply to code, then to teams (1, 7, 9).
  • Contracts and assumptions link design by contract, assertions, programming by coincidence and property-based tests (4, 7).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 1Broken windowsLet a team keep working on a 144-module codebase where every visible mess makes the next one more likely; compare ignoring broken windows, boarding them up, and fixing them at once.
  • Chapter 2Iterating the scheduleEstimate a project up front, then run it one iteration at a time and watch the forecast based on the team's measured pace close in on the real finish.
  • Chapter 2Orthogonality and the ripple of a changeWire up a six-module system with or without shared globals, cross-layer calls, duplicated rules and scattered authentication; change one requirement and count how many modules have to change.
  • Chapter 2A turtle-graphics mini-languageRun the book's Exercise 4 turtle program, write your own, see each line parsed into a command or an error, and add a new command by extending the command table.
  • Chapter 3Binary chopHunt a regression through a history of releases, or the record that crashes a program in a big dataset, stepping one at a time or chopping in half, and compare how many test runs each takes.
  • Chapter 4The blender contractDrive the book's Exercise 14 kitchen blender with its contract switched on or off, make the calls that break it, and see whether the caller or the blender is blamed.
  • Chapter 4Outrunning your headlightsCompare stopping distance with headlight throw using the book's NHTSA numbers, then choose how many steps a team commits to before getting feedback and see how much work each change of direction throws away.
  • Chapter 5The anagram pipelineType letters and watch them flow through the book's four transformations (subsets, signatures, dictionary lookup, grouping by length), then break a step and see an error tuple short-circuit the rest of the pipeline.
  • Chapter 5Table-driven state machinesFeed characters to the book's string-extracting state machine, or message types to its multipart parser, one event at a time, and watch the transition table pick each next state and action.
  • Chapter 6The last slice of pieStep two waiters through their code in any interleaving, with no lock, with a semaphore, or with a transactional get_pie_if_available, and count how often two customers are promised one slice.
  • Chapter 6The piña colada schedulerSchedule the book's twelve piña colada steps serially or by their dependencies, with one or more hands, and see where the one-minute liquefy frees the bartender for other work.
  • Chapter 7How does it scale?Set a baseline time and input size, grow the input, and compare how long algorithms of seven orders take, with the book's one-second example as a preset.
  • Chapter 7Hunt the falsifying exampleRun the book's stock-level property against the buggy and the fixed Warehouse with random items and quantities, watch cases until one fails, and shrink it to the smallest counterexample.
  • Chapter 8Free shipping over $50Build an order from the book's requirements example, switch what the $50 free-shipping threshold includes, and find the orders where the rule gives away more than the client meant.
  • Chapter 8Policy as code or as dataApply a stream of HR access-policy changes to a hard-coded check and to an access-control table, and count the code changes and redeploys each needs.
  • Chapter 9Saboteurs and state coveragePlant bugs in a small function and see which ones its test suite catches; then sample the book's a / (a + b) input space and see how rarely random tests find the one failing state.
  • Chapter 9Team size and communication pathsGrow a team and watch the pairwise communication paths multiply, with the book's ten-to-twelve guideline and its horde of fifty marked; then split a large group into small teams.

Key concepts

These ideas recur across chapters; each row lists the chapters that discuss them. The definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
Broken windowsSmall unrepaired imperfections signal that nobody cares and speed decay (software entropy). Fix them, or board them up, as soon as you see them.1 · 7 · 9
Knowledge portfolioTreat what you know like a financial portfolio: invest regularly, diversify, manage risk, buy low and rebalance.1 · 9
ETC (Easier to Change)Good design is design that is easier to change; the value behind most other principles.2 · 5 · 7 · 8
DRYEvery piece of knowledge has a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation. It's about knowledge and intent, not about copied text.2 · 7 · 9
OrthogonalityChanging one component doesn't affect others; independent, decoupled parts with focused responsibilities.2 · 5
ReversibilityThere are no final decisions; keep architecture flexible so choices of vendor or technology can be undone.2 · 8
Tracer bulletsA thin, real, end-to-end slice of the system that you keep and extend, as opposed to a throwaway prototype.2 · 9
Design by contractPreconditions, postconditions and class invariants that state what a routine requires and guarantees.4 · 7
Crash earlyA dead program does less damage than a crippled one; fail at the point of the problem.4 · 6
Don't outrun your headlightsTake small steps and get feedback before the next; don't predict far beyond what you can see.4 · 7 · 8
DecouplingShy code that talks only to what it knows directly: tell, don't ask; avoid train wrecks and global data.5 · 6
TransformationsThink of programs as pipelines that transform data, not as objects holding state.5
Temporal couplingCoupling in time: imposing an order or simultaneity that the problem doesn't require.6
Shared stateMutable data reachable from more than one place; every reader's view can go stale. Actors and blackboards avoid it.5 · 6
Programming by coincidenceRelying on luck and undocumented behaviour; the opposite of programming deliberately.7
Property-based testingGenerated inputs check contracts and invariants, so the computer tests assumptions you and your code share.7 · 9
Policy is metadataImplement the general mechanism and keep today's business rules as data.5 · 8
Pragmatic Starter KitVersion control, ruthless regression testing and full automation: the three legs of every project.3 · 9
